what: Redis keeps data in memory, so reads and writes come back in well under a millisecond. Apps use it as a cache, a counter, a lock, a queue or a leaderboard.
like: Like a sticky note on your monitor: far quicker than opening the filing cabinet (your database), but small - so you choose what goes on it.
why: Takes read load off the database and cuts response time
Ready-made data types: strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, streams and geo
Atomic counters and keys that expire on their own (TTL) - great for rate limits, sessions and locks

nodes.t: Event loop|one command at a time
Data in RAM|strings · hashes · sorted sets

steps.d: Your service sends a short command like GET user:42 over a TCP connection. Many services share one Redis.
Commands run one after another on a single main thread, so each one is atomic - no locks needed. Extra threads can handle network I/O.
The value comes straight from RAM in about 0.1-0.2 ms. A key can carry a TTL and disappear on its own.
With maxmemory set, Redis evicts keys by your policy - for example allkeys-lru (least recently used) or allkeys-lfu (least frequently used).
AOF appends every write and syncs once a second by default, so a crash loses about a second. RDB snapshots make backups and restarts quick.
Replicas copy writes in the background and take over if the primary fails. Cluster splits keys over 16,384 hash slots: CRC16(key) mod 16384 picks the node.

choices.d: Set maxmemory. For a pure cache pick allkeys-lru or allkeys-lfu; noeviction turns writes into errors once full.
Expire anything you can rebuild. Add a little random jitter so lots of keys don't expire in the same second.
Cache only: switch it off. Data you want back after a restart: AOF every second plus RDB snapshots.
A primary plus a replica is simplest. Move to Cluster when data or traffic outgrows one machine; multi-key commands then need keys in one slot, using {hash tags}.

instead.why: Plain key-value cache, multithreaded, no data types or persistence
Inside your app process: fastest, but every server keeps its own copy
A durable key-value database for data that must never be lost
A durable, replayable event log when Redis Streams are not enough

breaks.d: A hot key expires and thousands of requests rebuild it at once.
breaks.see: Database CPU and p99 latency jump right after an expiry
breaks.fix: Let one request rebuild while others wait, refresh early, add TTL jitter

breaks.d: One key gets most of the traffic, so one node maxes out.
breaks.see: One shard at 100% CPU while the others are calm
breaks.fix: A small local cache in front, or copies of the key (key:1 ... key:N)

breaks.see: evicted_keys climbing, or out-of-memory errors with noeviction
breaks.fix: The right policy, TTLs, smaller values, more memory or more shards

breaks.d: Replication is async, so a new primary can miss the last writes.
breaks.see: A replica promoted and the newest keys missing
breaks.fix: Keep the database as the source of truth; use WAIT for writes that matter

breaks.d: A big command holds the single thread.
breaks.see: Latency spikes for every client; SLOWLOG shows KEYS * or a huge range
breaks.fix: SCAN instead of KEYS, smaller ranges, heavy work kept off Redis

say: I'll put Redis in front of the database with cache-aside: read Redis first, and on a miss read the database and set the key with a TTL.
On writes I update the database first, then delete the cache key, so the next read loads fresh data.
Redis runs one command at a time, so INCR plus EXPIRE gives me an atomic counter per user for rate limiting.
If Redis is unavailable we fall back to the database behind a circuit breaker - slower for a moment, still working.

followups.q: How do you keep the cache and the database in sync?
followups.a: Write to the database, then delete the key rather than updating it. Short TTLs act as a safety net. For stricter needs, invalidate from the database change stream (CDC).

followups.q: What happens when a Redis node dies?
followups.a: A replica is promoted by Sentinel or Cluster. Replication is async, so the last moment of writes can be lost - fine for a cache, and the reason the database stays the source of truth.

followups.q: How would you hold 1 TB in cache?
followups.a: Redis Cluster: keys spread over 16,384 hash slots across many primaries, each with a replica. Clients route with CRC16(key) mod 16384, and {hash tags} keep related keys together.

followups.q: Why is Redis so fast on one thread?
followups.a: Data lives in memory, commands are tiny and one thread avoids lock overhead. The network is usually the limit, so pipelining helps more than extra CPU.

today: Redis is open source again since Redis 8 (2025), with AGPLv3 as one of its licences. Valkey, the Linux Foundation fork, speaks the same commands and many clouds offer it, so everything on this page applies to both.

check.q: Your cache is full and you want the popular keys to stay. Which policy?
check.why: LFU keeps the keys that are used often. noeviction would start rejecting writes instead.

check.q: With AOF syncing every second (the default), what can a crash lose?
check.a: About the last second of writes
check.why: everysec syncs once a second. RDB on its own could lose minutes, so many setups use both.

check.q: A popular key expires and the database suddenly spikes. What is that called?
check.why: Many requests miss at once and all rebuild the same value. Letting one request rebuild calms it.

check.q: Why can INCR count requests safely without a lock?
check.a: Commands run one at a time, so INCR is atomic
d: Redis locks the key on disk
The client retries until it wins
check.why: The single command thread means two INCRs never interleave.
